NeedleFinder 2026: Sub-Millimeter Catheter Reconstruction on MRI for Interstitial Gynecologic Brachytherapy in Seconds

Guillaume Pernelle, Paolo Zaffino, Lauren Barber, Alireza Mehrtash, Christiane Yeung, Tina Kapur, and Collaborators

October 2026 (Target Journal: Physics in Medicine & Biology)

Abstract

Objective. Interstitial gynecologic brachytherapy planned on MRI alone requires locating 15 to 30 thin plastic catheters on 3T T2-weighted images. Tracing them by hand takes tens of minutes while the patient is under anesthesia. Automatic methods based on voxel segmentation break catheters into fragments and mistake blood vessels for catheters. We set out to make catheter reconstruction automatic, accurate to below a millimeter, and fast enough to run during the procedure.

Approach. NeedleFinder 2026 works in three stages. Stage 0 computes an analytical 3D circular dark-core symmetry prior (S0S_0) and a 100% reference-free, tilt-safe axial field-of-view bound (k_lim_auto) that preserves 100.0% of in-FOV catheter depth. Stage 1 is a native-resolution 3D residual U-Net (NeedleUNet3D) self-supervised pre-trained on 51 strictly external pelvic T2W MRI volumes from 50 distinct subjects (combining 3D masked autoencoding with synthetic 3D susceptibility-tube pretext learning against real anatomical hard negatives) and trained with multi-rater supervision (CY+HT plus consensus-fused and soft-weighted LB/AMe traces on outer-training folds), 5-fold inner ensembling, and 4-view 3D test-time augmentation. Stage 2 traces candidate trajectories with native bidirectional Kalman tracking, a 4-layer triplet message-passing network, and collinear split-fragment stitching (102 stitched full-length trajectories), scores the whole implant bundle with a graph transformer pre-trained on 300 simulated bundles (SynthBrachy3T), and refines each distal tip with a dedicated 91-step (0.5 mm sub-slice Z-interpolated) 22-channel 3-block dilated 1D ResNet + 4-head self-attention axial localizer (Dedicated1DTipLocalizer). We evaluated the pipeline on 54 clinical 3T MRI scans (1,063 catheters: 759 long interstitial shafts and 304 short obturator tracks) under a strictly nested 5×55 \times 5 patient-level cross-validation protocol (25 inner models, zero outer-test leakage), against re-implementations of three published methods, against a second expert team across all 40 dual-traced scans, and on 48 public needle-free pelvic MRI scans.

Main results. At the pre-specified threshold τ=50%\tau = 50\%, NeedleFinder 2026 detected 91.4% of all 1,063 catheters (972/1,063) with 86.9% precision (972/1,118) and 89.1% F1 (89.1% with inner-OOF cross-fit; 89.4% F1 at τ=55%\tau = 55\%; 93.6% recall at τ=35%\tau = 35\%), outperforming our 2019-style 3D U-Net (83.1% F1, p=1.1×10−5p = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}), a native-resolution clDice ResUNet (38.7% F1, p=5.2×10−10p = 5.2 \times 10^{-10}), and a 2026-style structure-aware tracker (54.2% F1, p=3.0×10−10p = 3.0 \times 10^{-10}). On the 759 long interstitial shafts, it achieved 91.3% recall (92.5% with inner-OOF cross-fit; 94.7% at τ=35%\tau = 35\%), 88.7% obturator-adjusted precision, and 90.0% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} (90.5% inner-OOF cross-fit); on the 23-patient severe catheter-adhesion subgroup (571 catheters), it reached 91.3% F1 (91.8% inner-OOF cross-fit). The in-plane shaft error was 0.59±0.400.59 \pm 0.40 mm (0.470.47 mm median, 1.371.37 mm P95), and the 1D axial tip localizer cut 3D distal tip error from 7.707.70 to 6.236.23 mm mean (2.272.27 mm median, 27.2727.27 mm P95; 58.7%58.7\% within ≤3\le 3 mm), reaching 6.396.39 mm mean and 2.262.26 mm median even without SynthBrachy3T. Across all 40 dual-traced scans, NeedleFinder 2026 agreed more closely with the primary reference (0.58 mm mean / 0.47 mm median shaft, 5.26 mm mean / 2.10 mm median tip, 90.3% recall, 87.6% F1) than the two human expert teams agreed with each other (0.70 ± 0.58 mm mean / 0.49 mm median shaft, 6.28 mm mean / 3.24 mm median tip), and achieved 87.1% precision (87.6% F1) against the multi-rater union. Under a strictly leak-free few-shot protocol, F1 progressed from 75.3% (k=0k=0 analytical) and 78.2% (k=0k=0 zero-shot SynthBrachy3T, 83.4% on long shafts) to 79.7% (k=1k=1), 83.8% (k=5k=5, surpassing the 43-patient 3D U-Net baseline), 85.7% (k=10k=10), 86.6% (k=20k=20), and 89.1% (k=43k=43). On the 48 needle-free prostate MRI scans, the symmetry-gated full pipeline with zero MSD training exposure produced 16 false tracks (0.33/scan, 79.2% 0-FP, 91.7% ≤1\le 1-FP), and the self-supervised Stage 1 detector gated by Stage 0 produced 6 (0.125/scan, 87.5% 0-FP, 100.0% ≤1\le 1-FP). Uncached full-volume inference averaged 4.15 s on CPU (1.26 s on the 20 standard 320×256320 \times 256 scans, 5.85 s on the 34 high-resolution 640×416640 \times 416 / 768×768768 \times 768 scans) and 2.67 s on a GPU (0.68 s standard, 3.85 s high-resolution).

Significance. Automatic catheter reconstruction on clinical 3T T2W MRI achieves sub-millimeter shaft accuracy and sub-slice median tip accuracy within human inter-observer agreement in a few seconds per patient, turning tens of minutes of manual tracing into a brief verification step.

Plain-Language Summary

Some cancers of the cervix, vagina, and uterus are treated with brachytherapy: a tiny radioactive source is moved, for a few minutes, through thin plastic tubes placed inside the tumor. To aim the radiation, the treatment team must know exactly where each tube is. They find out with an MRI scan taken while the patient is still under anesthesia, and then trace every tube on the images by hand. With 15 to 30 tubes per patient this takes tens of minutes, and a small tracing error can change the planned dose, especially near organs where the dose changes quickly with position.

On an MRI scan a tube does not glow. It is a small dark dot, a few pixels wide, on each image slice. Blood vessels, air pockets, and the edges of muscles are also dark, so a computer can easily confuse them with tubes.

This paper presents NeedleFinder 2026, software that finds the tubes automatically. It works in three steps. First, a simple filter looks for small dark centers with brighter tissue all around them, the way a tube cross-section looks; it ignores broad one-sided edges, although it can still respond to blood vessels. Second, a 3D neural network—first pre-trained on 51 external pelvic MRI scans to distinguish synthetic catheter voids from real blood vessels and tissue borders—marks the center and direction of each tube on each slice. Third, two “graph” networks connect the marks from slice to slice into 3D curves, stitch fragments separated by single-slice dropouts, pull apart tubes that touch, score the whole bundle together to reject false curves, and pinpoint each tube’s deepest tip using a dedicated 1D axial profile network.

We tested it on 54 patients with 1,063 tubes using strictly nested cross-validation. It found 91.4 percent of all tubes (and up to 94.7 percent of the long interstitial shafts), and 86.9 percent of the tubes it reported matched an expert trace (89.1 percent F1). For the matched tubes, the typical sideways difference from the expert’s line was under half a millimeter (median 0.47 mm, mean 0.59 mm), which is smaller than the disagreement between two expert teams (median 0.49 mm, mean 0.70 mm); the deepest end of each tube had a median 3D difference of 2.27 mm (mean 6.23 mm), better than the 3.24 mm median disagreement between the two human teams. On average the software missed about 1.7 tubes per scan and reported about 2.7 extra tracks that had to be removed. It runs in 4.15 seconds on average on a desktop CPU (1.26 seconds on standard-resolution scans, 5.85 seconds on high-resolution scans) and 2.67 seconds on a graphics card. In practice, the physicist clicks one button and then checks the result, removes extra tracks, adds missing ones, and verifies tube ends. How much time this saves, and what it does to the treatment plan, has not yet been measured.

1 Introduction

1.1 The Clinical Problem

Brachytherapy delivers radiation from inside the body. For locally advanced cervical cancer it is the cornerstone of curative radiotherapy [1,2]. The EMBRACE-I study reported 92% local control at five years with a median dose of 90 Gy (EQD2) to the high-risk target volume [2], and EMBRACE-II now prescribes planning aims of 90 to 95 Gy while sparing the bladder, rectum, and sigmoid colon [1]. Reaching such doses in large or irregular tumors requires interstitial implants: in addition to a central tandem and a vaginal obturator or ring, 10 to 30 thin plastic catheters or needles are inserted into the tumor through a perineal template or freehand [3–5].

The tumor itself is best seen on T2-weighted (T2W) MRI, which GEC-ESTRO and consensus recommendations designate as the reference for target delineation and set reconstruction requirements for [6,7]. MRI-based applicator reconstruction with marker-filled catheters was established for cervical cancer in 2009, with inter-observer standard deviations below 2 mm [8]. Historically, clinics took both an MRI and a CT scan and registered the two, which adds its own uncertainty to the reconstruction [9], and practical guidance for hybrid implants still advises a CT in addition to the MRI because plastic needles are hard to see on MRI [10]. The AAPM Task Group 303 report describes how to implement MRI in HDR brachytherapy from simulation to treatment [11], the Medical Physics Practice Guideline 13.a lists MRI among the accepted planning modalities [12], and MRI-only interstitial workflows have been shown to be feasible [13,14]. Positive-contrast line markers make the catheter lumen visible on T1-weighted or balanced sequences [13,15] and are listed as required equipment in published implementation guides [16], and zero-echo-time sequences show empty catheters directly [14,17], but both need an additional series fused to the T2W images. Identifying the source path on the T2W series alone remains a recognized challenge [18]; for rigid applicators, direct reconstruction on T2W MRI is in fact more precise than library-based or fused workflows [19], but interstitial needles have no library model.

Finding the catheters on MRI is the central technical challenge of an MRI-only workflow [4,20]. The dose from the 192^{192}Ir source falls steeply with distance: organ-at-risk dose parameters change by up to 5 to 6% per millimeter of applicator displacement [21], applicator shifts beyond 1.5 mm can change the rectal D2cc by more than 10% [22], and in MRI-only cervical implants a systematic 1 mm error along the source path already changes organ-at-risk doses significantly [23]. Swapping two catheters during digitization changes prostate, urethra, and rectum dose metrics by 5 to 20% [24], and needle reconstruction uncertainty alone shifts the urethral dose by about 3 Gy in prostate implants [25]. Manual reconstruction is itself error-prone: with electromagnetic tracking as the reference, 23% of 265 needle reconstructions in ultrasound-guided prostate implants deviated by 2 mm or more [26]. Yet a 2 mm plastic catheter contains no mobile water protons and shows up on T2W MRI only as a small dark hole, a few pixels across, surrounded by anatomy full of other dark structures: blood vessels, air, calcifications, and the fascial planes between muscles. Tracing 15 to 30 catheters slice by slice therefore takes tens of minutes, 46 minutes on average in one MRI-only gynecologic series [27], within a template-based implant procedure of about 100 minutes under anesthesia [28].

1.2 Key Terms

Readers outside medical physics may find the following definitions useful.

  • Catheter, needle, shaft, tip. We use catheter and needle interchangeably for the thin plastic tubes. The shaft is the length of the tube visible on the scan; the tip is its deepest end.
  • Digitization or reconstruction. Tracing the 3D path of each catheter on the images so the planning software knows where the source will travel.
  • Slice, voxel, in-plane. An MRI volume is a stack of 2D images (slices). Each 3D picture element is a voxel. In-plane means within one slice; here the in-plane pixel is 0.31 to 0.88 mm while slices are 1.2 to 6.0 mm thick.
  • Recall, precision, F1. Recall is the fraction of true catheters the method found. Precision is the fraction of reported catheters that were real. F1 combines the two into one score that is high only when a method both finds the real catheters and avoids inventing extra ones. As an illustration, with 10 real catheters, 8 found and 2 false reports, recall, precision, and F1 are all 80%.
  • Shaft error and tip error. The distance, in millimeters, between the automatic trajectory and the expert’s trajectory, measured in-plane along the shaft and in 3D at the tip.
  • Nested cross-validation, out-of-fold. The 54 patients were split into 5 outer groups (43–4443\text{--}44 training vs. 10–1110\text{--}11 test patients per fold). Within each outer fold, early stopping, temperature calibration, and optionally inner-OOF upstream feature generation for downstream stackers use a strictly disjoint 80/20 inner split or 5-fold inner cross-fitting, so no test patient’s images or labels influence training, checkpoint selection, or threshold calibration.
  • Inter-observer variability. How much two expert teams disagree when they trace the same scan independently. It gives context for how closely an automatic method can be expected to agree with any one expert.

1.3 Previous Work

Automatic catheter digitization has gone through three generations. Two recent systematic reviews cover the field [20,29].

Model-based tracking (2013 to 2019). The BWH program of 3T MR-guided gynecologic brachytherapy in the AMIGO suite, which produced the cohort used here, was described in 2012 together with the first image-analysis tools for catheter identification [30] and open-source 3D Slicer modules for template and obturator registration [31]. Our first catheter tracker on this cohort seeded each catheter with one click at its tip, searched inside a sequence of expanding 3D cones, and fitted a Bézier curve; 93 of 101 catheters in 10 patients were traced correctly at 0.3 s per catheter [32]. Mastmeyer et al. [3] constrained the cone search with a mechanical rod-and-spring catheter model, reaching 1.49 mm mean Hausdorff distance on 760 catheters in 54 patients, still from a manual tip click; a first version of that model, presented at MICCAI 2015, reached 1.40 mm mean error on the 101 catheters of the 2013 set [33]. Template-geometry-assisted reconstruction on MRI has been described for commercial interstitial templates [34], and on ultrasound 3D Hough transforms localized single needles with about 1 mm endpoint accuracy in vivo [35]. On CT, seeded region growing constrained by a spline model digitized template implants to within 0.4 mm of manual digitization [36], and thresholding followed by density-based clustering reaches 0.3 mm for rigid applicators [37], but MRI offers no such intensity threshold. Related model-to-image registration reconstructs rigid applicators on MRI within inter-observer variability [38], and line fitting by RANSAC digitizes straight needles on CT [39]. These methods are interpretable but need manual initialization and fail when catheters bend sharply or cross dark anatomy.

Voxel segmentation with heuristic post-processing (2019 to 2026). To remove manual initialization, Zaffino et al. [4] trained an ensemble of 3D U-Nets to segment catheter voxels on 50 clinical T2W scans with 826 catheters, then clustered the voxels with DBSCAN and removed small islands. It reached a voxel Dice of 0.60, a mean distance error of 2.0 mm, 6.7% false-positive and 1.5% false-negative clusters, in 2 to 9 minutes per patient. Convolutional segmentation, often nnU-Net based [40], has since been applied to CT brachytherapy of the cervix, prostate, and breast [41–49], to MRI-guided prostate implants [50–52], to single needles on interventional MRI [53,54], to transrectal ultrasound [55–61], and to gynecologic MRI with line markers [27] or with applicator mesh alignment [62]. Even with topology-preserving losses, from the Betti-number loss [63] to clDice [64] and skeleton recall [65], pure voxel segmentation has two failure modes on T2W MRI: a one-slice signal dropout splits one catheter into two to four fragments, and dark vessels and tendons are segmented as short false catheters. The ultrasound literature documents the same pattern: accuracy collapses on artifact-laden catheters [60] and tips are much harder than shafts [59]. Keypoint heatmap regression, the choice made for our Stage 1, has recently been shown to localize an interventional needle on MRI more accurately than mask segmentation of the same images [66]. Electromagnetic or active MR tracking avoids the imaging problem altogether, at the cost of dedicated hardware and sequences in the operating room [28,67–73]; crossed catheter paths were already identified as a common failure of image-based digitization in the BWH program when active tracking was introduced [68].

Structure-aware tracking and graph networks (2022 to 2026). On CT, Xiao et al. [74] identified two further problems: catheter adhesion, where shafts touch or overlap on consecutive slices so that greedy trackers swap or merge them, and the scarcity of annotated clinical data. They proposed an implant-region gating module (IRGM) that suppresses features outside the implant, a direction-constrained 3D Hough transform for initialization, synchronous cost-based inward tracking across slices, cubic polynomial smoothing, and synthetic-to-real training, on 38 patients and 203 fractions. Their companion work handles needle adhesion in dense CT seed implants by detecting tips and handles [75]. Outside brachytherapy, message-passing networks have replaced greedy linking in tracking-by-detection [76,77], transformers predict graphs of curvilinear structures directly from images [78], and synthetic-to-real training has been shown to transfer to real needle detection [79]. Applied to MRI masks, however, a mask-driven tracker still turns vessels inside the implant region into false catheters, and nothing in it asks whether the full set of trajectories makes sense as one implant.

Open data. No public needle or catheter dataset for brachytherapy exists [80], and the AI literature in brachytherapy remains largely retrospective and single-center [29]. The public pelvic MRI scans we use for self-supervised pretraining and the false-alarm test come from the Medical Segmentation Decathlon [81].

1.4 Contributions

This paper combines the strengths of all three generations on the full 54-patient, 1,063-catheter BWH cohort, to our knowledge the largest annotated MRI cohort for interstitial gynecologic brachytherapy.

  1. A three-stage architecture with five methodological upgrades. An analytical dark-core symmetry prior and 100% reference-free axial template locator (Stage 0); a 3D residual U-Net pre-trained on 51 external pelvic T2W MRI volumes with physics-guided synthetic susceptibility tubes and anatomical hard negatives, then fine-tuned with dual-observer multi-rater consensus supervision (Stage 1); and two graph networks plus a dedicated 1D axial tip localizer (Stage 2): native seed tracking with a triplet message-passing network, adhesion-aware duplicate merging, and collinear split-fragment stitching, followed by a tip-aware bundle graph transformer and a 91-step dilated 1D ResNet + self-attention axial tip localizer (Dedicated1DTipLocalizer).
  2. A strictly nested 5×55 \times 5 comparison. We re-implemented three published approaches and evaluated all methods and ablations under strictly nested patient-level 5-fold cross-validation (plus 5×55 \times 5 inner out-of-fold Stage 1 cross-fitting), on the whole cohort, on the 759 long active-dwell shafts, and on the 23 patients with severe catheter adhesion.
  3. Three clinically relevant checks. Agreement with experts compared with agreement between experts across all 40 doubly traced scans (against both individual teams and their de-duplicated union); leak-free label efficiency as a function of how many annotated training patients (k∈{0,1,5,10,20,43}k \in \{0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 43\}) are available to fine-tune the bundle-scoring stage; and false alarms on 48 public pelvic MRI scans containing no catheters.

Table 1 summarizes the data. The primary cohort is 54 intraoperative 3T T2W turbo spin-echo MRI scans acquired during MRI-guided interstitial gynecologic brachytherapy in the AMIGO suite at Brigham and Women’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA) with Institutional Review Board approval [3,4,32]. It consolidates the patients of our 2013 and 2019 studies, of which 48 scans could be recovered with their reference traces, and adds 6 new implants. Expert medical physicists traced 1,063 reference trajectories (9 to 42 per patient): 759 full-depth interstitial catheters from the primary annotation set (CY), which we call long shafts, and 304 short obturator and partial-field-of-view tracks from the secondary set (HT). In-plane pixel size ranges from 0.31 to 0.88 mm and slice thickness from 1.2 to 6.0 mm.

Xiao et al. [74] analyzed separately the fractions in which catheters touch or overlap. We define a severe-adhesion subgroup in the same spirit: the 23 of 54 patients in which at least 4 long, or at least 6 of all, reference catheters pass within 3.0 mm of another catheter on shared axial slices. All 571 catheters of these patients are evaluated; 191 of them (166 long) lie within 3.0 mm of a neighbor, and 233 do across the whole cohort.

Two further datasets serve as checks and external pre-training sources. All 40 doubly traced scans were contoured independently by two expert teams (CY+HT, 723 trajectories = 505 CY long + 218 HT short/obturator; LB/AMe, 513 trajectories, of which 460 are long); the 424 strict long-to-long matched pairs and 476 all-catheter matched pairs within 3.5 mm define the human inter-observer floor, and the de-duplicated union of both teams contains 759 trajectories. For self-supervised 3D representation learning and zero-needle specificity testing, we use 51 external pelvic 3T T2W MRI volumes from 50 distinct subjects: all 48 pelvic T2W scans of the public Medical Segmentation Decathlon prostate task [81] (MSD Task05_Prostate; 0.60 to 0.75 mm in-plane, 3 to 4 mm slices) plus 3 non-benchmark BWH pelvic T2W series from 2 distinct subjects (Case 061 [2 series] and Case 100 Prostate [1 series], zero patient overlap with the 54 benchmark cases).

2.2 Stage 0: Analytical Dark-Core Symmetry Prior and Reference-Free Cropping

The physical idea is simple. On an axial slice a catheter cross-section is a dark core that is surrounded by brighter tissue in every direction, whereas a fascial plane or a muscle border is dark on one side only. Stage 0 turns this into a parameter-free score S0(x,y,z)S_0(x,y,z), computed slice by slice in multi-threaded native Rust.

For each voxel 𝐩\mathbf{p} on slice zz we sample six diameters through 𝐩\mathbf{p} at angles θd=dπ/6\theta_d = d\pi/6, d∈{0,…,5}d \in \{0, \dots, 5\}, and four physical radii r∈ℛ={1.35,1.85,2.5,3.3}r \in \mathcal{R} = \{1.35, 1.85, 2.5, 3.3\} mm, converting each radius to pixels with the in-plane spacing. For diameter dd and radius rr the darker of the two ring samples is kept, md,r=min(I(𝐩+r𝐮d),I(𝐩−r𝐮d)),m_{d,r} = \min\!\big(I(\mathbf{p} + r\mathbf{u}_d),\; I(\mathbf{p} - r\mathbf{u}_d)\big), so that a one-sided edge, where one end of the diameter stays dark, produces a small md,rm_{d,r}. The six values are sorted, m(1),r≤…≤m(6),rm_{(1),r} \le \dots \le m_{(6),r}, and the ring brightness is a robust weighted order statistic that still tolerates one dark neighbor, Sring(𝐩)=maxr∈ℛ[0.45m(2),r+0.55m(3),r].S_{\text{ring}}(\mathbf{p}) = \max_{r \in \mathcal{R}} \big[0.45\, m_{(2),r} + 0.55\, m_{(3),r}\big]. The response S0S_0 grows with the positive contrast between this ring brightness and the 3×33 \times 3 smoothed center intensity and with the relative darkness of the core, and is normalized per volume. Candidate centers are the local maxima of S0S_0 after non-maximum suppression.

Before running Stage 1, a 100% reference-free axial template locator (k_lim_auto) identifies the caudal entry slice directly from the 3D intensity volume and S0(x,y,z)S_0(x,y,z): it detects the caudal-to-cranial transition from the air/template saturation drop (p90 intensity transition) and the emergence of clustered dark-core candidates within the central field of view, setting the lower axial crop bound with a mean difference of −0.06-0.06 slices (median 0.00.0, IQR 1.01.0 slice) relative to clinical scene annotations while never consulting reference trajectories. Stage 0 takes 0.41 s per full volume on average on an 8-core CPU (0.12 s on standard 320×256320 \times 256 scans and 0.59 s on high-resolution 640×416640 \times 416 / 768×768768 \times 768 scans).

2.3 Stage 1: Self-Supervised and Multi-Rater Multi-Head 3D U-Net

Resampling the scan to 1 mm isotropic voxels, as most pipelines do, discards the fine in-plane detail that separates a 2 mm catheter void from its surroundings when the native pixels are 0.3 to 0.9 mm. Working on the native grid instead, a standard 3×3×33 \times 3 \times 3 convolution mixes information over up to ten times more distance along zz than in-plane. Stage 1 (NeedleUNet3D, Figure 2a) therefore operates on the native grid, uses 3×3×33 \times 3 \times 3 residual blocks with squeeze-and-excitation attention at four scales (24, 48, 96, and 144 channels), pools only in-plane at the first two scales so that the thick slice axis is not downsampled early, and adds a dilated convolution at the deepest scale. Its input has six channels: the normalized intensity, the Stage 0 dark-core response and ring-symmetry contrast, the smoothed intensity, and the normalized slice position and in-plane distance from the field-of-view center.

The network predicts four outputs:

  1. Tubular mask PmaskP_{\text{mask}}: focal binary cross-entropy, weighted 19-fold on catheter voxels and up-weighted on bright Stage 0 responses that are not catheters, plus soft Dice on the tubular label around each reference trajectory.
  2. Centerline peak PpeakP_{\text{peak}}: a sharp 2D Gaussian (σ=0.70\sigma = 0.70 mm) at the sub-pixel intersection of each catheter with the slice, trained with a mean-squared-error loss up-weighted 26-fold at the peaks. Two touching catheters whose masks merge still produce two distinct peaks.
  3. Direction field (Vx,Vy)=(Δx/Δz,Δy/Δz)(V_x, V_y) = (\Delta x/\Delta z, \Delta y/\Delta z): the local slope of the trajectory, trained with a smooth L1L_1 loss inside the mask, with an additional term that penalizes slice-to-slice inconsistency of the predicted direction.
  4. Obturator channel PobtP_{\text{obt}}: a dedicated segmentation of the large central obturator and tandem, so that its lumen and rim do not spawn false needles.

To improve feature discrimination on dark pelvic anatomy without leaking test-patient information, NeedleUNet3D undergoes two training phases:

  • External pelvic MRI pre-training with synthetic susceptibility tubes and anatomical hard negatives. The full 3D U-Net (encoder, decoder, and task heads) is pre-trained for 45 epochs across the 51 external pelvic T2W MRI volumes from 50 distinct subjects (48 public MSD Task05_Prostate volumes + 3 non-benchmark BWH pelvic T2W volumes, zero patient overlap with the 54 benchmark cases). During each iteration, physics-guided 3D cubic-spline susceptibility tubes (dark core with realistic T2W partial-volume rim, dropout pockets, and variable curvature) are injected into the needle-free pelvic volumes alongside 3D masked volume patches. The network minimizes a joint loss ℒSSL=ℒtube+0.30ℒMAE\mathcal{L}_{\text{SSL}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{tube}} + 0.30\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{MAE}}, where ℒtube\mathcal{L}_{\text{tube}} supervises tubular mask, peak, and 3D direction regression on the synthetic tubes while penalizing non-implanted high-symmetry pelvic structures (S0>0.25S_0 > 0.25: vessels, fascia, obturator internus borders) as explicit anatomical hard negatives, and ℒMAE\mathcal{L}_{\text{MAE}} reconstructs masked 3D tissue patches (reaching 0.8670.867 validation Dice on synthetic tubes).
  • Multi-rater consensus supervision. On the 40 dual-annotated training scans (CY+HT and LB/AMe) within each outer training fold (n=43–44n=43\text{--}44 patients), consensus-matched trajectories (n=465n=465 pairs within ≤3.5 mm\le 3.5\text{ mm}) are supervised along their inverse-variance precision-weighted centerline (weight 1.151.15), primary-only (CY) trajectories at weight 1.001.00, secondary-only (LB/AMe) trajectories at soft weight 0.550.55, and secondary cranial tip slices with a soft axial Gaussian tip kernel.

As an ablation we also evaluate AxialTransUNet3D, which adds multi-head self-attention layers along the slice axis at the deepest encoder level and the bottleneck.

2.4 Stage 2: From Slice Detections to a Coherent 3D Bundle

Stage 2 answers three questions: which detections on neighboring slices belong to the same catheter, which of the resulting 3D curves are real, and exactly where each catheter terminates along the slice axis.

2.4.1 Stage 2A: Native Seed Tracking, Triplet Message Passing, and Collinear Stitching

On each slice, local maxima of PpeakP_{\text{peak}} and of S0S_0 become nodes with a 16-dimensional feature vector (normalized position, PmaskP_{\text{mask}}, PpeakP_{\text{peak}}, S0S_0, local 3×33 \times 3 intensity statistics, predicted slope, and obturator proximity). Directed edges connect nodes across 1 to max(4,24 mm/Δz)\max(4, 24\text{ mm}/\Delta z) slices. An edge is kept when its chord slope is at most 0.56 and its in-plane displacement lies within 2.8+0.14Δz2.8 + 0.14\,\Delta z mm of the position predicted by the Stage 1 direction field, or within 3.5+0.22Δz3.5 + 0.22\,\Delta z mm outright. Each edge carries 12 features (displacement, chord slope, and agreement with the predicted direction).

Two consecutive links can each look plausible on their own yet form an abrupt bend when considered together; the network therefore scores each link using information from the links entering and leaving its two nodes. NeedleSliceMPNN is a 4-layer triplet-collinearity message-passing network (hidden size 64). Each layer updates an edge from its own features, the embeddings of its two nodes, and attention-aggregated messages from the edges entering and leaving each of those nodes, so that the update sees the incoming and outgoing chords together and can discourage a kink. The network outputs refined sub-pixel offsets (δxi,δyi)(\delta x_i, \delta y_i) and node and edge probabilities.

Candidate 3D tracks themselves are traced in native code: from each Stage 0 and Stage 1 seed, a bidirectional Kalman tracker follows the catheter slice by slice in both directions and trims it from the inside out where the evidence ends. Tracks that run within 1.65 to 2.05 mm of each other, depending on their confidence, are merged as duplicates; the margin is chosen so that genuinely adhering twins survive. Next, collinear axial split-fragment stitching and extrapolation-aware deduplication reconnects trajectories broken across 1 to 3 slices by local signal dropouts or vessel crossings: pairs of non-overlapping or slightly overlapping track fragments (axial gap ≤20 mm\le 20\text{ mm}, overlap ≤6 mm\le 6\text{ mm}) whose linearly extrapolated positions at their shared axial midpoint agree within ≤2.2 mm\le 2.2\text{ mm} with a 3D slope-vector difference ≤0.14\le 0.14 are merged into a single full-length trajectory (102102 stitched trajectories across the 54 cases), while split fragments that lie within ≤2.1 mm\le 2.1\text{ mm} along ≥72%\ge 72\% of a longer high-confidence shaft are absorbed. The surviving tracks are passed to Stage 2B.

2.4.2 Stage 2B: Bundle Graph Transformer, Dedicated 1D Axial Tip Localizer, and Synthetic Pre-Training

After Stage 1, recall is above 95% (97.5% on long shafts), but each patient still carries about seven false tracks along vessels and obturator edges; Stage 2A removes more than half of them. Real catheters have a property these false tracks lack: they form a bundle. They enter through a common template or corridor, run roughly parallel to the obturator axis, keep at least 2 mm apart, and their tips form a coherent surface over the target.

Each candidate trajectory is summarized by a list of 26 measurements, its token (length, linear-fit residual, 75th-percentile S0S_0 and PmaskP_{\text{mask}}, PpeakP_{\text{peak}}, PobtP_{\text{obt}}, the three message-passing probabilities, agreement between models, the deviation of its entry position and slope from the bundle median, and the contrast gradient at its cranial end), together with 8 pairwise features between trajectories (minimum 3D clearance, mean in-plane separation, angular divergence, zz-overlap, and duplicate indicators). The TipAwareBundleGraphTransformer applies two edge-biased attention layers over neighboring trajectories and one global self-attention layer over the whole bundle. It outputs three logits (a recall-oriented score, a strict one-to-one score, and a long-shaft one-to-one score), combined into a confidence pmp_m, alongside an initial bundle-context tip offset. An implant-region gate inspired by the IRGM of Xiao et al. [74] is applied geometrically: the implant center is the median in-plane position of candidates with confidence ≥55%\ge 55\%, the implant radius is the 98th percentile of their distances plus 16 mm, and candidates outside this radius require 22 points higher confidence.

Because a single scalar offset from bundle summary statistics cannot resolve fine sub-slice signal drop-offs or air-pocket artifacts at the cranial end of a catheter, Stage 2B incorporates a Dedicated 1D Axial Tip Localizer (Dedicated1DTipLocalizer, Figure 2b). Along the cranial-most trajectory tangent of each candidate, the localizer samples a 91-step axial profile over [−25.0,+20.0] mm[-25.0, +20.0]\text{ mm} at 0.5 mm0.5\text{ mm} sub-slice intervals. At every step it extracts 22 multi-scale tubular, intensity, and anatomical features: center and 3×33 \times 3 / 5×55 \times 5 ring T2W intensities, local annular contrast (r=3 vs. 1r=3\text{ vs. }1, r=5 vs. 1r=5\text{ vs. }1), first- and second-order axial gradients (∂z\partial_z, ∂zz\partial_{zz}), Stage 0 S0S_0 center/max/drop, Stage 1 PmaskP_{\text{mask}} and PpeakP_{\text{peak}} center/max/drop, obturator probability PobtP_{\text{obt}}, normalized axial coordinate, step indicators, and bundle-relative zz-depth. A 3-block dilated 1D ResNet (hidden width 48, kernel size 5, dilations 1,2,41, 2, 4) followed by 4-head 1D Self-Attention processes the 91-step sequence and drives a dual prediction head: a 91-bin soft-argmax termination probability distribution combined with a Smooth-L1L_1 continuous residual offset head, supervised with Gaussian target distributions (σ=1.25 mm\sigma = 1.25\text{ mm}), focal peak classification, and huberized L1L_1 displacement loss. Each accepted trajectory (pm≥τp_m \ge \tau, default τ=50%\tau = 50\%) has its cranial tip updated by the 1D localizer and is smoothed with a cubic polynomial fit in zz (Poly3).

To study zero-shot and low-label bundle scoring, we also built SynthBrachy3T, a generator of 300 synthetic candidate-trajectory bundles with the same 26 node and 8 edge features as real candidates (12 to 23 true long shafts per bundle, 30% with an adhering twin 1.65 to 2.75 mm away, 2 to 8 short obturator tracks, 3 to 11 split duplicates, and 4 to 14 vessel-like false tracks). Stage 2B can be pre-trained on SynthBrachy3T and then fine-tuned purely on the clinical training bundles of the current outer fold.

3 Experimental Setup

3.1 Strictly Nested Cross-Validation Protocol and Baselines

Every learned component, every ablation, and every baseline is trained and evaluated under a strictly nested 5×55 \times 5 patient-level out-of-fold (OOF) protocol across the 54 patients, eliminating three subtle sources of optimistic bias present in standard stacked evaluations:

  1. Disjoint inner validation for early stopping and calibration. For each outer fold f∈{0,…,4}f \in \{0, \dots, 4\} (43–4443\text{--}44 outer-train patients, 10–1110\text{--}11 outer-test patients), outer-train patients are partitioned deterministically into an 80% inner-train subset (34–3534\text{--}35 patients) and a 20% inner-validation subset (99 patients). Stage 1 U-Net checkpoint selection, Stage 2A MPNN and Stage 2B Graph Transformer early stopping, Dedicated1DTipLocalizer model selection, and confidence temperature scaling are performed exclusively on the 99 inner-validation patients; the outer-test fold is touched exactly once at final evaluation.
  2. 100% reference-free axial cropping (k_lim_auto). Every outer-test volume is cropped using the automatic k_lim_auto template-plane locator derived solely from the raw 3D MRI and Stage 0 S0S_0 volume, with zero fallback to clinical scene files or ground-truth trajectory coordinates.
  3. Inner-OOF cross-fitting of Stage 1 features (4c). In a standard 2-stage pipeline (4a, 4b), Stage 2 is trained on outer-train patients using Stage 1 probability maps produced by the outer-fold Stage 1 model (which trained on those same outer-train patients’ images). To verify that this causes zero stacking optimism, we also trained 5×5=255 \times 5 = 25 inner-fold Stage 1 NeedleUNet3D models so that every outer-train patient receives strictly out-of-fold Stage 1 probability maps when training Stage 2A, Stage 2B, and Dedicated1DTipLocalizer (configuration 4c in Table 2).

We re-implemented three published approaches on the identical outer folds and k_lim_auto bounds:

  • PMB 2019: 3D U-Net + DBSCAN [4]. Volumes resampled to 1 mm isotropic, segmented by a 3D U-Net, then grouped by principal-axis estimation, DBSCAN clustering, and spline fitting.
  • ResUNet + clDice + skeleton [40,64]. A native-resolution 3D residual U-Net trained with binary cross-entropy, soft Dice, and the centerline-Dice loss, followed by morphological skeletonization, connected components, and polynomial centerline fitting.
  • Xiao 2026 Sync-Track [74]. Implant-region gating, direction-constrained 3D Hough and PCA initialization, synchronous inward tracking, and cubic smoothing, evaluated both on our out-of-fold segmentation masks and on the reference masks (an oracle upper bound).

3.2 Metrics and Statistics

Predicted and reference trajectories are matched one-to-one with the Hungarian algorithm (SciPy linear_sum_assignment): pairs whose mean in-plane distance over the shared slices exceeds 3.5 mm are forbidden before solving, so the assignment first maximizes the number of valid pairs and then minimizes their distance. Error distributions are computed over matched pairs; a patient with no matched pair contributes fixed penalty values (3.5 mm shaft, 10 mm curve, 20 mm tip and HD95) to the per-patient arrays used in the statistical tests. We report:

  1. Detection: recall, precision, and F1 under strict one-to-one matching (plus obturator-adjusted precision PadjP_{\text{adj}} and F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} when evaluating the 759 long active-dwell shafts alone, so predictions that match a valid secondary short/obturator reference track are not counted as false positives).
  2. Shaft error EshaftE_{\text{shaft}}: the in-plane distance between the two curves at 40 evenly spaced positions along their shared length, summarized by mean, standard deviation, median, interquartile range, and 95th percentile.
  3. 3D curve distance DavgD_{\text{avg}} and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance HD95\text{HD}_{95}, computed symmetrically on 50 resampled points per curve.
  4. Tip error EtipE_{\text{tip}}: the 3D Euclidean distance between the predicted and reference deepest (cranial) tip.

Calibration and reason-coded decisions. Every candidate track in the Stage 2B pool (1,6831,683 candidates across the 54 patients) is also treated as a binary prediction: it is a real catheter if its mean in-plane distance to some reference trajectory over their shared slices is at most 3.5 mm, and its predicted probability is the Stage 2B confidence pmp_m. Over all candidates we report a reliability diagram, the expected calibration error (ECE, ten equal-width bins), and the Brier score; temperature scaling is fitted on the inner-validation split of each fold and applied to the outer-test fold. Each decision of the decoder carries a typed reason code (kept, below threshold, duplicate of a kept track, outside the implant region, low dark-core symmetry), and for every discarded candidate that is a real catheter we record whether that catheter is already covered by a kept track (redundant) or lost.

Following GEC-ESTRO and AAPM guidance on reporting brachytherapy uncertainties [82], reconstruction discrepancies are reported as distributions (median, interquartile range, and 95th percentile) and separated from observer variation. Differences between methods are tested over the 54 patients with paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and 95% confidence intervals come from 1,000 patient-level bootstrap resamples.

3.3 Computing Environment, Software, and Code

Training and the nested 5×55 \times 5 benchmarks ran on a Linux workstation (Arch Linux) with a 24-core AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7965WX, 256 GB of RAM, and two NVIDIA GPUs (GeForce RTX 4090, 24 GB, and RTX 4070 Ti SUPER, 16 GB) using Python 3.12/3.13, PyTorch 2.4/2.11, SciPy 1.16, NumPy 2.4, and ONNX Runtime 1.23. The Stage 0 kernel is written in Rust (crate needlefinder_rust, multi-threaded with the standard library, exposed to Python through a C interface and ctypes, compiled in release mode with link-time optimization). For clinical deployment, the trained Stage 1, Stage 2B, and 1D tip localizer networks are exported to ONNX and run with ONNX Runtime inside an extension for 3D Slicer 5.10 [83]; no GPU is required.

The 3D Slicer extension, the Rust kernel, and the exported models are available at https://github.com/needlefinder/NeedleFinder. All training, nested cross-validation, statistical analysis, SynthBrachy3T, and figure/table generation scripts are archived in vault/paper/benchmarks.

Table 2 reports the complete benchmark. Part A compares all methods on the whole cohort (54 patients, 1,063 catheters) and on the severe-adhesion subgroup (23 patients, 571 catheters); Part B reports the step-by-step architectural ablations and threshold sweep on the same nested folds; and Part C evaluates the 759 full-depth active-dwell interstitial shafts (CY). Figure 3 shows the full per-catheter error distributions.

Five findings stand out.

Voxel segmentation alone over-fragments. The ResUNet + clDice baseline finds almost every catheter (92.4% recall) and is accurate where it matches (0.43 mm median shaft error), but it reports 4,015 fragments across the 54 volumes. Its precision is 24.5% and its F1 38.7%. Signal dropouts along the shaft cut one catheter into several pieces, and dark veins become extra tracks.

Structure-aware tracking needs a clean mask. On the reference masks (Table 2, Part B, last row), the Xiao 2026 tracker achieves 97.7% recall, 90.0% F1, and 0.11 mm median shaft error: given a perfect mask, synchronous tracking separates touching shafts well. On out-of-fold MRI masks its F1 drops to 54.2% (precision 39.2%), because vessels inside the implant region still become tracks and the adapted pipeline has no bundle-level step that rejects them. Tracking alone does improve on skeletonization, by 15.5 F1 points on the whole cohort.

NeedleFinder 2026 achieves the highest F1 and lowest tip error across all evaluated methods. At the pre-specified default threshold τ=50%\tau = 50\%, NF 2026 + SynthBrachy3T + 1DTip (4b) reaches 91.4% recall (972/1,063972/1,063), 86.9% precision (972/1,118972/1,118), and 89.1% F1 (rising to 89.4% F1 at τ=55%\tau = 55\%, 89.2% F1 at τ=60%\tau = 60\%, and 93.6% recall at τ=35%\tau = 35\% or 94.5% recall at τ=25%\tau = 25\%). The gains over all three published baselines are highly statistically significant: +6.0 F1 points over PMB 2019 (89.1%89.1\% vs. 83.1%83.1\%, p=1.1×10−5p = 1.1 \times 10^{-5}), +34.9 F1 points over Xiao 2026 (p=3.0×10−10p = 3.0 \times 10^{-10}), and +50.4 F1 points over ResUNet + clDice (p=5.2×10−10p = 5.2 \times 10^{-10}). On matched catheters, the in-plane shaft error is 0.59±0.40 mm0.59 \pm 0.40\text{ mm} mean (0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median, 0.36 mm0.36\text{ mm} IQR, 1.37 mm1.37\text{ mm} P95), the 3D symmetric curve distance DavgD_{\text{avg}} is 3.20±4.87 mm3.20 \pm 4.87\text{ mm} mean (1.00 mm1.00\text{ mm} median), and HD95\text{HD}_{95} is 15.36±22.87 mm15.36 \pm 22.87\text{ mm} mean (3.11 mm3.11\text{ mm} median). Most notably, the Dedicated 1D Axial Tip Localizer and collinear fragment stitching reduce 3D distal tip error to 6.23±10.49 mm6.23 \pm 10.49\text{ mm} mean (2.27 mm2.27\text{ mm} median, 4.93 mm4.93\text{ mm} IQR, 27.27 mm27.27\text{ mm} P95), significantly outperforming PMB 2019 (10.75 mm10.75\text{ mm} mean / 3.39 mm3.39\text{ mm} median, p=1.7×10−8p = 1.7 \times 10^{-8}), ResUNet + clDice (10.08 mm10.08\text{ mm} mean / 3.10 mm3.10\text{ mm} median, p=2.3×10−7p = 2.3 \times 10^{-7}), and Xiao 2026 (15.65 mm15.65\text{ mm} mean / 6.04 mm6.04\text{ mm} median, p=6.2×10−10p = 6.2 \times 10^{-10}). Nearly three-fifths (58.7%, 571/972571/972) of matched catheters have a 3D tip error ≤3.0 mm\le 3.0\text{ mm} (within roughly one slice thickness), while 16.7% (162/972162/972) exceed 10 mm10\text{ mm} (100100 caudal undershoots where dark signal fades early and 6262 cranial overshoots into fundal dark pockets). Across the 54 patients, the method misses 91 reference trajectories (1.7 per patient1.7\text{ per patient}) and reports 146 unmatched tracks (2.7 per patient2.7\text{ per patient}). On the 759 long interstitial shafts (Table 2, Part C), NF 2026 reaches 91.3% recall (693/759693/759), 88.7% obturator-adjusted precision (79.1%79.1\% strict long-only precision), and 90.0% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} (84.8%84.8\% strict F1) at τ=50%\tau = 50\%—and 94.7% recall (719/759719/759) at τ=35%\tau = 35\%—with 0.57 mm0.57\text{ mm} mean (0.45 mm0.45\text{ mm} median) shaft error and 2.41 mm2.41\text{ mm} median tip error.

Strict 5×55 \times 5 inner out-of-fold cross-fitting confirms zero stacking optimism, and clarifies the exact role of SynthBrachy3T. Training Stage 2 on strictly out-of-fold inner Stage 1 predictions (4c, NF 2026 + SynthBrachy3T + Inner-OOF Cross-Fit) yields 92.3% recall (981/1,063981/1,063), 86.1% precision, and 89.1% F1 (0.59 mm0.59\text{ mm} mean / 0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median shaft error; 6.25 mm6.25\text{ mm} mean / 2.24 mm2.24\text{ mm} median tip error), and achieves the highest obturator-adjusted F1 on long shafts (90.5% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}, 92.5%92.5\% recall, 7.17 mm7.17\text{ mm} mean tip error) and on the severe-adhesion subgroup (91.8% F1, 94.6%94.6\% recall, 89.1%89.1\% precision). Furthermore, once the self-supervised multi-rater Stage 1, collinear fragment stitching, and Dedicated1DTipLocalizer are in place, our purely clinical pipeline without SynthBrachy3T (4a) already reaches 88.7% F1 (92.5%92.5\% recall, 85.3%85.3\% precision; 90.2%90.2\% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} on long shafts) and 6.39 mm6.39\text{ mm} mean / 2.26 mm2.26\text{ mm} median tip error. At the full 43-patient training budget, adding SynthBrachy3T (4b) provides a modest refinement to 89.1%89.1\% F1 (+0.41 pp+0.41\text{ pp}, p=0.32p = 0.32) and 6.23 mm6.23\text{ mm} mean / 27.27 mm27.27\text{ mm} P95 tip error (p=0.17p = 0.17, patient-paired mean tip error 6.02→5.91 mm6.02 \to 5.91\text{ mm}); as shown below, the primary value of SynthBrachy3T lies in the zero-clinical-label (k=0k = 0) regime.

The advantage is largest when catheters touch. On the 23 severe-adhesion patients (571 catheters), NF 2026 reaches 91.3% F1 (93.2% recall, 89.6% precision, 0.58 mm0.58\text{ mm} mean / 0.46 mm0.46\text{ mm} median shaft error, 7.08 mm7.08\text{ mm} mean / 2.51 mm2.51\text{ mm} median tip error) under 4b and 91.8% F1 (94.6% recall, 89.1% precision, 0.57 mm0.57\text{ mm} mean / 0.46 mm0.46\text{ mm} median shaft error, 2.47 mm2.47\text{ mm} median tip error) under inner-OOF cross-fitting (4c), compared with 90.8%90.8\% without synthetic pre-training (4a), 86.3%86.3\% for PMB 2019 (p=5.4×10−4p = 5.4 \times 10^{-4}), 63.9%63.9\% for Xiao 2026 (p=2.1×10−6p = 2.1 \times 10^{-6}), and 48.4%48.4\% for ResUNet + clDice (p=2.4×10−7p = 2.4 \times 10^{-7}).

4.2 Contribution of Each Stage and Leak-Free Learning From Few Patients

Figure 4(a) traces the progression across stages (Table 2, Part B). Analytical Stage 0 alone (1a) achieves 83.2% recall and 75.3% F1 (0.65 mm0.65\text{ mm} median shaft error, 3.92 mm3.92\text{ mm} median tip error). Multi-rater SSL Stage 1 with directional tangent linking (2a) raises recall to 95.3% (97.5%97.5\% on long shafts) with 72.1% precision (82.1% F1) and cuts median shaft error to 0.45 mm0.45\text{ mm} and median tip error to 2.98 mm2.98\text{ mm}. Stage 2A native seed tracking, triplet MPNN scoring, and collinear split-fragment stitching (3c) lift precision by 12.1 points to 84.2% (86.4% F1, 6.48 mm6.48\text{ mm} mean / 2.33 mm2.33\text{ mm} median tip error). Finally, Stage 2B bundle graph-transformer pruning and Dedicated1DTipLocalizer reach 88.7% F1 without synthetic bundles (4a) and 89.1% F1 with SynthBrachy3T (4b, 4c).

Figure 4(b) evaluates strictly leak-free Stage 2B clinical label efficiency: for each support budget k∈{0,1,5,10,20,43}k \in \{0, 1, 5, 10, 20, 43\}, the Stage 2B bundle graph transformer is fine-tuned exclusively on outer_train[:k] clinical patient bundles of that fold (with zero score blending from any full-fold k=43k=43 clinical model). With zero clinical bundle labels (k=0k = 0), analytical Stage 0 alone gets 75.3% F1 (77.1%77.1\% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} on long shafts), while the zero-shot SynthBrachy3T-pretrained Stage 2B (0_synth_zeroshot, k=0k = 0) reaches 78.2% F1 (+2.85 pp+2.85\text{ pp} overall, and 83.4%83.4\% F1adjF1_{\text{adj}} [+6.3 pp+6.3\text{ pp}] with 94.9%94.9\% recall on long shafts). Fine-tuning Stage 2B on a single annotated clinical patient (k=1k = 1) reaches 79.7% F1 (84.3%84.3\% long F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}); 5 annotated patients (k=5k = 5) reach 83.8% F1 (86.5%86.5\% long F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}, 2.33 mm2.33\text{ mm} median tip error), already surpassing the fully supervised 43-patient PMB 2019 3D U-Net baseline (83.1% F1); 10 patients (k=10k = 10) reach 85.7% F1 (88.1%88.1\% long F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}); 20 patients (k=20k = 20) reach 86.6% F1 (88.8%88.8\% long F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}); and all 43 patients (k=43k = 43) reach 89.1% F1 (90.0%90.0\% long F1adjF1_{\text{adj}}).

Figure 5 illustrates the stages on two difficult out-of-fold test cases (Case 017 with 23 predicted trajectories vs. 26 reference, and Case 031 with 20 predicted vs. 23 reference). Stage 0 highlights every round dark core in the pelvis, including vessels. Stage 1 suppresses background anatomy and resolves adjacent catheters into separate peaks even where their masks touch. Stage 2 then stitches dropouts, prunes false tracks, localizes the cranial tips, and outputs smooth 3D bundles with no swapped identities.

Because a catheter is only a few pixels wide and slices are thick, two experts clicking centerlines never agree perfectly; inter-observer discrepancies of about 0.6 mm have been reported for breast implants, and more than a third of prostate needles differ by over 1 mm between observers [84,85], and algorithms within that range are considered clinically equivalent to a second observer [38,58]. Table 3 measures this across all 40 doubly traced clinical scenes (CY+HT, 723 trajectories = 505 CY long + 218 HT short/obturator; LB/AMe, 513 trajectories, of which 460 are long) and compares it with NeedleFinder 2026 evaluated out-of-fold on the exact same 40 scenes.

Comparing the two human teams on long shafts (LB/AMe 460 long vs. CY 505 long), 424 pairs match one-to-one within ≤3.5 mm\le 3.5\text{ mm} (84.0% recall, 92.2% strict precision [93.6%93.6\% obturator-adjusted], 87.9% strict F1 [88.5%88.5\% obturator-adjusted]), with a shaft discrepancy of 0.70±0.58 mm0.70 \pm 0.58\text{ mm} mean (0.49 mm0.49\text{ mm} median, 0.52 mm0.52\text{ mm} IQR, 1.90 mm1.90\text{ mm} P95) and a 3D tip discrepancy of 6.28±10.67 mm6.28 \pm 10.67\text{ mm} mean (3.24 mm3.24\text{ mm} median, 4.33 mm4.33\text{ mm} IQR, 23.13 mm23.13\text{ mm} P95). Across all 723 CY+HT reference trajectories, LB/AMe matches 476 pairs (65.8%65.8\% recall, 92.8%92.8\% precision, 77.0%77.0\% F1; 0.73 mm0.73\text{ mm} mean / 0.50 mm0.50\text{ mm} median shaft discrepancy, 6.30 mm6.30\text{ mm} mean / 3.21 mm3.21\text{ mm} median tip discrepancy).

Evaluated out-of-fold across all 40 scenes, NeedleFinder 2026 (τ=50%\tau = 50\%, 768 predicted trajectories) matches 653 of 723 CY+HT trajectories (90.3% recall, 85.0% precision, 87.6% F1; rising to 92.5% recall at τ=35%\tau = 35\%) with a mean shaft error of 0.58±0.39 mm0.58 \pm 0.39\text{ mm} (0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median, 0.36 mm0.36\text{ mm} IQR, 1.33 mm1.33\text{ mm} P95) and a 3D tip error of 5.26±9.10 mm5.26 \pm 9.10\text{ mm} mean (2.10 mm2.10\text{ mm} median, 3.95 mm3.95\text{ mm} IQR, 21.56 mm21.56\text{ mm} P95)—lower than the inter-observer disagreement between the two human teams in mean, median, and 95th-percentile error for both shafts and tips. Even more revealingly, when evaluated against the de-duplicated union of both expert teams (CY+HT ∪\cup LB/AMe, 759759 union trajectories), NeedleFinder 2026 matches 669 trajectories (88.1% recall, 87.1% precision, 87.6% F1, 0.59 mm0.59\text{ mm} mean / 0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median shaft error, 5.44 mm5.44\text{ mm} mean / 2.17 mm2.17\text{ mm} median tip error): 16 trajectories that appeared to be false positives against CY+HT alone are in fact genuine catheters independently traced by LB/AMe, raising precision by +2.1 pp+2.1\text{ pp}. Against LB/AMe alone (513 traces), NeedleFinder 2026 matches 465 trajectories (90.6% recall, 0.77 mm0.77\text{ mm} mean / 0.51 mm0.51\text{ mm} median shaft error, 3.97 mm3.97\text{ mm} median tip error; unadjusted precision is 60.5%60.5\% solely because LB/AMe omitted most of the 218 HT short obturator tracks that NF 2026 detects).

4.4 Confidence Calibration, Reason-Coded Decisions, and Failure Analysis

A confidence score is useful to the physicist if it ranks candidates reliably. Figure 6(a) shows the reliability diagram over all 1,683 candidate tracks: the expected calibration error (ECE) is 0.093 raw and 0.082 after inner-fold temperature scaling (0.047 over kept tracks; Brier score 0.119). Figure 6(b) breaks down the reason-coded decisions of the decoder across the 1,683 candidates.

A systematic audit of all residual detection and tip errors for NF 2026 (4b, τ=50%\tau = 50\%) across the 54 patients identifies their exact physical causes:

  • False positives (146 unmatched predictions across 54 patients, 2.70 per patient): 66 (45.2%) are short peripheral vascular or fascial false tracks (<35< 35 mm axial span) along the obturator internus or paravaginal venous plexus; 48 (32.9%) are long vascular or fascial mimics (≥35\ge 35 mm); 16 (11.0%) are genuine unannotated catheters confirmed by the independent LB/AMe observer team; 9 (6.2%) are residual unmerged duplicate fragments within 3.5 mm of a matched trajectory; and 7 (4.8%) are central tandem or obturator rim artifacts within 12 mm of the implant center.
  • False negatives (91 missed reference trajectories, 1.69 per patient): 66 are long CY shafts (8.7% miss rate) and 25 are short HT obturator tracks (8.2% miss rate). Among the 91 misses, 47 (51.6%) lie in severe-adhesion clusters where an adjacent trajectory passes within 3.5 mm and suppresses the weaker twin during deduplication, 21 (23.1%) are ultra-short partial-volume tracks (≤25\le 25 mm or ≤5\le 5 slices), and 23 (25.3%) suffer severe T2W susceptibility signal dropout across the mid-shaft.
  • Residual tip outliers (>10> 10 mm 3D tip error on 162 of 972 [16.7%] matched catheters): 100 (61.7%) are caudal undershoots (Δz<0\Delta z < 0, track stops early where dark susceptibility contrast fades into bright parametrial tissue) and 62 (38.3%) are cranial overshoots (Δz>0\Delta z > 0, tracker continues into a dark bowel loop, air pocket, or vessel at the uterine fundus).

A method deployed in the clinic must not invent catheters when none are present. We evaluated seven pipeline configurations on all 48 public pelvic 3T T2W MRI scans of MSD Task05_Prostate containing zero catheters (Table 4, Figure 7a). Without Stage 0 dark-core radial symmetry gating, raw Stage 1 NeedleUNet3D tangent tubes produce 306306 false tracks (6.38 FP/scan6.38\text{ FP/scan}), the unpruned Stage 0 + Stage 1 candidate pool contains 294294 (6.12 FP/scan6.12\text{ FP/scan}), and the ungated Unified NF 2026 bundle transformer leaves 197197 (4.10 FP/scan4.10\text{ FP/scan}) at τ=50%\tau = 50\% and 171171 (3.56 FP/scan3.56\text{ FP/scan}) at τ=60%\tau = 60\%. Activating the analytical Stage 0 3D multi-radii circular dark-core symmetry gate suppresses >92%> 92\% of false vascular and fascial tracks: on models with zero exposure to MSD during training, Stage 1 U-Net + Stage 0 radial gate produces only 18 false tracks across 48 scans (0.38 FP/scan0.38\text{ FP/scan}, median 00, 64.6%64.6\% [31/4831/48] 0-FP scans, 97.9%97.9\% [47/4847/48] ≤1\le 1-FP scans) and the Frozen Unified NF 2026 + Dark-Core Gate (τ=50%\tau = 50\%) produces 16 false tracks (0.33 FP/scan0.33\text{ FP/scan}, median 00, 79.2% [38/4838/48] 0-FP scans, 91.7% [44/4844/48] ≤1\le 1-FP scans). When Stage 1 is also pre-trained with self-supervised synthetic susceptibility tubes and anatomical hard negatives (Clean SSL + Multi-Rater Stage 1 + Stage 0 gate), false tracks drop to 6 across all 48 volumes (0.125 FP/scan0.125\text{ FP/scan}, median 00, max 11, 87.5% [42/4842/48] 0-FP scans, and 100.0% [48/4848/48] ≤1\le 1-FP scans; as noted in Table 4, the 48 MSD volumes were part of the unlabeled/synthetic-tube SSL pre-training background pool for this row with zero clinical needle labels, whereas the 0.33–0.38 FP/scan0.33\text{--}0.38\text{ FP/scan} rows had zero exposure to MSD).

Speed follows from the native-code and ONNX design (Figure 7b, c). Measured end-to-end across all 54 uncached clinical volumes, Stage 0 runs in multi-threaded native Rust in 0.41 s0.41\text{ s} mean (0.12 s0.12\text{ s} on standard-resolution scans, 0.59 s0.59\text{ s} on high-resolution scans), Stage 1 runs in 2.28 s2.28\text{ s} on an 8-core CPU (1.88 s1.88\text{ s} on GPU) via strided/cropped ONNX Runtime inference, Stage 2A runs in 1.22 s1.22\text{ s} on CPU (0.54 s0.54\text{ s} on GPU), and Stage 2B (including Dedicated1DTipLocalizer and Poly3 smoothing) runs in 0.24 s0.24\text{ s}. Full-volume uncached reconstruction takes 4.15±2.38 s4.15 \pm 2.38\text{ s} mean (5.35 s5.35\text{ s} median) on an 8-core desktop CPU—specifically 1.26 s1.26\text{ s} mean (1.26 s1.26\text{ s} median) on the 20 standard-resolution (320×256×28–40320 \times 256 \times 28\text{--}40) scans and 5.85 s5.85\text{ s} mean (5.94 s5.94\text{ s} median) on the 34 high-resolution (640×416×112–160640 \times 416 \times 112\text{--}160 / 768×768×64768 \times 768 \times 64) scans—and 2.67±1.44 s2.67 \pm 1.44\text{ s} mean (3.45 s3.45\text{ s} median) on a single RTX 4090 GPU (0.68 s0.68\text{ s} standard-resolution, 3.85 s3.85\text{ s} high-resolution). That is one to two orders of magnitude faster than our 2019 pipeline (2 to 9 minutes reported; 14.8 s14.8\text{ s} in our optimized re-implementation) [4] and 2.8–4.3×2.8\text{--}4.3\times faster than Xiao et al. (11.6 s11.6\text{ s}) [74].

5.1 Where This Work Sits in the Literature

Table 5 places NeedleFinder 2026 among published catheter reconstruction studies on CT, ultrasound, and MRI. CT and ultrasound solve an easier imaging problem: metal needles, air-filled lumens, or bright specular reflections give very high contrast, so segmentation networks reach shaft errors of 0.1 to 0.7 mm on CT [45,49,74] and 0.1 to 0.6 mm on ultrasound [56,58]. On T2W MRI without contrast markers, a catheter is a 2 mm dark hole that looks like a vessel, on slices 1.2 to 6 mm thick; the best published MRI results are 0.74 to 0.97 mm shaft error on gynecologic implants, obtained with line markers or with CT-derived reference reconstructions [27,62] and 0.75 to 0.93 mm on prostate implants [50,52]. NeedleFinder 2026 reaches a median shaft error of 0.47 mm (0.59 mm0.59\text{ mm} mean; 0.45 mm0.45\text{ mm} median / 0.57 mm0.57\text{ mm} mean on long active-dwell shafts) and a median 3D tip error of 2.27 mm (6.23 mm6.23\text{ mm} mean) on T2W MRI alone, on the largest annotated MRI cohort to date.

The head-to-head comparison in Table 2 explains why neither voxel segmentation [4,40,64] nor mask-driven tracking [74] is enough on MRI, and why the three-stage architecture works. Skeletonizing a mask cannot bridge a one-slice dropout, and it turns every vessel blob into a track. Tracking bridges the gaps but still trusts the mask. NeedleFinder 2026 resolves these bottlenecks through five complementary mechanisms: Stage 0 rejects one-sided anatomical edges before learning takes place and automatically locates the template plane (k_lim_auto); Stage 1 combines self-supervised pre-training on external pelvic MRI (with synthetic susceptibility tubes and anatomical hard negatives) and multi-rater consensus supervision to regress sharp centerline peaks that stay separate when masks merge; Stage 2A bridges 1-to-3 slice dropouts via triplet message passing and collinear fragment stitching; Stage 2B judges each trajectory in the context of the entire 15 to 30 catheter bundle; and the 91-step dilated 1D ResNet + self-attention axial localizer (Dedicated1DTipLocalizer) pinpoints the distal termination directly from sub-slice multi-scale tubular profiles.

5.2 What It Means in the Clinic, and Limitations

NeedleFinder 2026 is a one-click module in 3D Slicer [83] that runs in a few seconds without a GPU (4.15 s4.15\text{ s} mean on CPU, 1.26 s1.26\text{ s} on standard scans, 2.67 s2.67\text{ s} on GPU). It changes the physicist’s task from tracing 15 to 30 catheters slice by slice, which takes tens of minutes, into a brief verification step: click Detect Needles, inspect the 3D bundle and the axial intersections, remove the 2 to 3 extra tracks per scan, add the 1 to 2 missed catheters, and verify the tips. Because the in-plane shaft error (0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median, 0.59 mm0.59\text{ mm} mean) is smaller than the disagreement between two human expert teams (0.49 mm0.49\text{ mm} median, 0.70 mm0.70\text{ mm} mean; Table 3)—and 16 apparent false positives on the 40 dual-traced scans are actually real catheters traced by the second observer team—the shafts themselves rarely require manual adjustment.

Several limitations remain. First, while Dedicated1DTipLocalizer and collinear fragment stitching cut the mean 3D tip error from 10.75 mm10.75\text{ mm} (PMB 2019) and 15.65 mm15.65\text{ mm} (Xiao 2026) to 6.23 mm6.23\text{ mm} (2.27 mm2.27\text{ mm} median, with 58.7%58.7\% of tips within ≤3.0 mm\le 3.0\text{ mm}, better than the 3.24 mm3.24\text{ mm} human inter-observer median), 16.7%16.7\% (162/972162/972) of matched catheters still have a tip error above 10 mm10\text{ mm} (27.27 mm27.27\text{ mm} P95), driven by caudal undershoots where susceptibility contrast fades (100100 cases) or cranial overshoots into fundal air/bowel pockets (6262 cases). Along-axis tip uncertainty is fundamentally bounded by slice thickness (1.2–6.0 mm1.2\text{--}6.0\text{ mm}), and each millimeter of along-axis displacement changes the target D90 by 1 to 2.5% [86]. Thin-slice isotropic 3D T2W sequences (SPACE or VISTA, ≤1 mm\le 1\text{ mm}), zero-echo-time sequences [14,17], or multi-contrast T1W+T2W inputs are the natural next step to suppress the remaining tip tail. Second, all 54 clinical brachytherapy scans come from a single institution and one 3T scanner. While the 48 external MSD scans demonstrate strong zero-needle specificity (0.33–0.38 FP/scan0.33\text{--}0.38\text{ FP/scan} with zero MSD exposure during training, and 0.125 FP/scan0.125\text{ FP/scan} when MSD volumes are included in the unlabeled/synthetic-tube SSL pre-training pool), a prospective multi-center study across 1.5T, 3T, and low-field systems [87] from multiple vendors is needed to establish cross-scanner generalization. Third, we have not yet measured the wall-clock editing time or the downstream dosimetric impact (ΔD90\Delta D_{90}, ΔD2cc\Delta D_{2\text{cc}}) of the residual errors in a clinical treatment planning system. Fourth, our ablation shows that once multi-rater SSL Stage 1, collinear stitching, and the 1D axial tip localizer are included, SynthBrachy3T provides its main gain in the zero-label (k=0k=0) regime (+2.85 pp+2.85\text{ pp} F1 overall, +6.3 pp+6.3\text{ pp} on long shafts) while adding only +0.41 pp+0.41\text{ pp} F1 (p=0.32p=0.32) at the full 43-patient training budget.

6 Conclusion

Evaluated under strictly nested 5×55 \times 5 patient-level out-of-fold cross-validation with 100% reference-free axial cropping (k_lim_auto) across 54 clinical 3T T2W MRI scans (1,0631,063 catheters), NeedleFinder 2026 achieves 89.1% F1 (91.4% recall, 86.9% precision; 92.3% recall and 89.1% F1 under 5×55 \times 5 inner-OOF Stage 1 cross-fitting), 0.59±0.40 mm0.59 \pm 0.40\text{ mm} mean (0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median) in-plane shaft error, and 6.23±10.49 mm6.23 \pm 10.49\text{ mm} mean (2.27 mm2.27\text{ mm} median) 3D distal tip error, executing in 4.15 s4.15\text{ s} on an 8-core desktop CPU (1.26 s1.26\text{ s} on standard-resolution scans, 5.85 s5.85\text{ s} on high-resolution scans) and 2.67 s2.67\text{ s} on a GPU. On the 759 full-depth active-dwell shafts it reaches 91.3% recall (94.7%94.7\% at τ=35%\tau = 35\%) and 90.0% obturator-adjusted F1 (90.5% with inner-OOF cross-fitting), and on the 23 patients with severe catheter adhesion it reaches 91.3%–91.8% F1. Across all 40 doubly annotated clinical scans, its agreement with the primary expert team (0.47 mm0.47\text{ mm} median shaft error, 2.10 mm2.10\text{ mm} median tip error) is tighter than the agreement between two independent human expert teams (0.49 mm0.49\text{ mm} median shaft error, 3.24 mm3.24\text{ mm} median tip error), its bundle-scoring stage surpasses a 43-patient 3D U-Net baseline using only k=5k = 5 annotated clinical patients (83.8%83.8\% vs. 83.1%83.1\% F1), and its false-positive rate on 48 catheter-free public pelvic MRI scans is reduced to 0.33–0.380.33\text{--}0.38 per scan without MSD training exposure and 0.1250.125 per scan (87.5%87.5\% zero-FP scans, 100%100\% ≤1\le 1-FP scans) with self-supervised anatomical hard-negative pre-training.

Data Availability

The 54 clinical MRI scans and their expert traces were acquired at Brigham and Women’s Hospital under Institutional Review Board approval and contain protected health information; they cannot be shared publicly. De-identified trajectory annotations and per-patient evaluation results may be made available by the corresponding author on reasonable request, subject to institutional and ethics approval. The 48 needle-free scans are the public Medical Segmentation Decathlon prostate task (Task05_Prostate), available at http://medicaldecathlon.com [81]. The SynthBrachy3T generator is released with the code, so the 300 synthetic bundles can be regenerated from a fixed random seed.

Code Availability

The 3D Slicer extension, the Rust Stage 0 kernel, and the exported ONNX and NumPy models are available at https://github.com/needlefinder/NeedleFinder under an open-source license. Training, nested cross-validation, statistical analysis, SynthBrachy3T, prediction-export, and figure-generation code is collected in the vault/paper/benchmarks directory of the same repository and will be made public on publication.
